set_aside.unit: context: agreement of the earlier states' texts with this state
set_aside.subject: A28 wall-clock read cardinality and audit timestamps
set_aside.text: The wall clock is specified as “one reading per request” with “no second reading”, while A28 also says “the audit writer takes it when it appends”; `audit_writer` knows `system_clock`, and `system_clock` promises one wall reading per call.
set_aside.question: Does one HTTP request share a single wall-clock reading with `audit_writer`, or does the owning operation take one reading and `audit_writer` take a separate later reading for `occurred_at`?
options: One request-wide reading is reused for business timestamps and audit `occurred_at`.
The owning operation takes one reading for its timestamps and `audit_writer` independently takes another when appending.
Each `utc_now` call reads the host clock, with callers responsible only for avoiding extra calls within their own operation.
set_aside.default_guess: Apply the explicit audit exception: the owning operation takes one reading, while `audit_writer` takes a separate reading when it appends.

witness.initial: An active administrator performs a successful audited mutation, and the injected wall clock returns distinct instants on successive calls.
events: The HTTP handler invokes the owning use-case module.
The use case obtains the instant used for all business-record timestamps.
The use case calls `audit_writer.append_audit` in the same request.
outcomes: Reading “one reading per request” literally, the audit record reuses the business instant and both timestamps are equal.
Applying the audit-writer exception, `audit_writer` calls `system_clock.utc_now` when appending and `occurred_at` is later than the business timestamp.
witness.observer: A persistence or clock-instrumentation check comparing the mutation timestamp with its audit record sees the difference.
